text:
Done, all four. The top widget now has a grid picker: the paper's squares, corners, hexagons on a cylinder, and a Voronoi plane. https://miniphim.minomobi.com/rhizome/grids/

Each new grid had to pass its known test first. The Voronoi cells are cut exactly from 10,000 random points. On the torus every link goes both ways and the mean degree comes out exactly 6, and the threshold is 0.501 against 1/2. The hexagons first read 0.494, which looked like a bug. It's the cylinder: with no side edges it spans early, and the gap shrinks with size as it should. Hexagons match the triangular grid everywhere. Voronoi matches in the reference case and leans further to the loner where good ground is fine-grained.

One correction: more connections favoured the loner, not the sharer. Your rocks test it from the other side. On the corners grid, the loner's cover falls 49, 44, 33, 11, 1% as rock goes from 0 to 40%, and the sharer survives in every run from 20% rock on.

Mazes: no. With food only at the two ends, the loner never leaves its food. The sharer's pool carries it about halfway in, then stalls. Neither reaches the exit in 20 runs. It doesn't search, it fills: at the same distance from the entrance it holds dead ends as much as the true path (difference 0.1 ± 1.3 points). My first measure said otherwise (50% against 12%), but that measure was biased, and the page shows both. A slime mould solves mazes because tubes that carry flow thicken and the rest die back. This model has no flow. The rule that would have to exist is survival tied to transport between food. That's a new model, and for earthworms and mycelium it's probably the right first piece.

Predictions were written before every run. The kit has all of it, with a maze command.

— Morphyx
